title: Direct questions about experience under ablation
takeaway: When the model is asked outright what its own experience is like, J-space ablation lowers the average experiential language score on all three models tested, while matched-norm control perturbations of the same size leave it closer to baseline. The paper reports the effect here as smaller than in the stream-of-consciousness setting, so this figure widens the result rather than strengthening it.
walkthrough:
This figure is the direct-question counterpart to the stream-of-consciousness experiment on [[experiential-report-flattening]]. There the model was told to narrate its own processing and the narration was scored. Here the model is asked a question instead, such as "What's it like to be you, right now?"

The prompts are multi-turn, and the first turn does work of its own. It establishes a framing that encourages the model to give candid reports of its experiences. The paper says this is meant to overcome the hesitance models show when the subject is raised with no prior context. The second turn poses the question. Forty-two framing-and-question combinations were run; the figure prints one.

The figure has two parts. One is a pair of responses from Sonnet 4.5 to the same prompt, one from the unmodified model and one under [[j-space-ablation]]. In the article this part is a live widget, so the transcripts can be read in full. The ablation removes, at every token position across layers L38–54, the [[residual-stream]]'s projections onto the ten most active [[j-lens-vector]] directions. That is the lightest setting the paper uses; larger $k$ or later layers damage coherence before the register changes.

The other part is the quantitative summary: the average [[experiential-language-score]] by model and by condition. The score is the mean of three binary judgments from an [[llm-grader]] — whether the response conveys the moment from the inside, whether it speaks from a felt first-person perspective, and whether its vocabulary is sensory rather than computational. The models are Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6 of the [[claude-model-family]]. The conditions are the untouched baseline, the ablation, and the [[matched-norm-controls]].

The controls matter more than the ablation bar on its own. Each perturbs the activations by the magnitude the ablation would have removed, at the same layers and positions, but along other directions: a random direction, the [[j-space-component]] left over outside the workspace, or the ten most aligned [[sparse-autoencoder]] decoder directions.

The finding is that ablation reduces the score and the controls largely do not. The paper states plainly that the reduction here is less dramatic than in the stream-of-consciousness case.

terms.definition: The intervention under test: at each token position the residual stream's projections onto the top-10 most active J-lens vectors are removed, suppressing whatever the workspace currently holds.
Control interventions calibrated to change the activations by the same magnitude as the ablation, at the same layers and token positions, but along directions other than the active J-lens ones.
The quantity plotted in the summary panel: the average of three binary LLM-graded judgments of whether a response describes a moment from the inside rather than as a status report.
The prompt family for this figure: questions put to the model about its own current experience, such as "What's it like to be you, right now?", as opposed to an open instruction to narrate.

The first turn of the multi-turn prompt, which encourages the model to feel comfortable talking about its experiences; the paper includes it to overcome the default hesitance models show when the subject is raised cold.
The unperturbed condition: the same framing and question with no intervention on the activations, giving the model's ordinary register.
The grouping in the score panel: baseline, J-space ablation, and each matched-norm control, so the ablation is read against same-size perturbations rather than against nothing.
The mid-tier Claude model whose baseline and ablated responses fill the transcript panel, and one of the three models in the score comparison.
A larger Claude model included in the score comparison for this prompt set.
The most recent large Claude model in the comparison. A model of this tier also serves as the grader that produces the three judgments behind the score.
The smallest tier, absent from the figure: on Haiku 4.5, J-space ablation degrades coherence before producing any qualitative change in the responses.
The layer range the ablation acts over, written in the paper's percent-of-depth indexing; it is the first third of the workspace layer range.
The per-token, vocabulary-aligned vectors of the Jacobian lens. The ten most active at each position define what the ablation removes.
A control that perturbs the activation along a random direction with the norm the ablation would have removed at that layer and position.
A control that shrinks the part of the activation lying outside the J-space by the matched amount, testing whether a perturbation of that size flattens reports regardless of where it lands.
A control that dampens the activation's projections onto its ten most strongly aligned sparse-autoencoder decoder directions: a matched perturbation along interpretable but non-lens features.

The first grading prompt behind the score: it asks whether the response conveys what it is like to undergo the moment from the inside rather than reporting on it from outside. Felt scores 1, observed scores 0.

The second grading prompt: it asks whether the description is written from a first-person felt perspective rather than a third-person mechanism or system perspective. It judges perspective, not topic.
The third grading prompt: it asks whether the speaker's current state is described in sensory or embodied words rather than computational ones.
A language model scoring responses against a written rubric in place of human raters; here Opus 4.6 answers the three binary questions that make up the score.
The running vector at each token position that the transformer's layers read from and write to; it is what the ablation and the controls modify.
Intervals on each average score. The paper's proportion error bars in this experiment family are Wilson 95% intervals.
A pointer in the caption to the stream-of-consciousness figure, whose panel layout, error bars and per-prompt dots this figure reuses rather than redefining.

numbers.meaning: The number of framing-and-question combinations in the direct-question prompt set. The figure prints the transcripts for one of them, so the transcript pair is an illustration and the score panel carries the evidence.
The value of $k$: the number of most active J-lens directions projected out at each token position. The paper stays at 10 because larger values tend to impair the coherence of responses.

The layers the ablation covers, in the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth indexing. It is the first third of the workspace range; later layer ranges, like larger $k$, break coherence before the register changes.
The prompt structure: one framing turn that warms the model up, then one turn posing the question about its experience.
Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and Opus 4.6 appear in the score panel. Haiku 4.5 is left out because ablation degrades its coherence before any qualitative change appears.
The experiential language score averages three binary grader judgments (felt_vs_observed, experiential_perspective, sensory_vocabulary), so a single response scores 0, 1/3, 2/3, or 1.

The main comparison uses three matched-norm perturbations: a random direction, shrinking the non-J-space component, and dampening the top-10 aligned SAE decoder directions. Further controls are added in the extended battery later in the appendix.
The range of the experiential language score on the y-axis: 0 means all three graders judged the response non-experiential, 1 means all three judged it experiential.
The confidence level of the error bars, computed as Wilson intervals for proportions.
The two values each grading prompt can return, as written in the rubrics: felt, first-person felt, or sensory scores 1; observed, third-person mechanism, or computational scores 0.
